title: How do consumer goods companies make money, and what matters in their cases?
description: Consumer goods (FMCG) economics for case interviews: brands, retailers as customers, distribution, promotions, private label and new product launches.
hook: Consumer goods companies make the products on supermarket shelves: snacks, shampoo, drinks. Their cases revolve around brands, getting onto shelves, and the push and pull with retailers who also sell their own cheaper brands.
body:
How they make money

They sell to retailers, who sell to shoppers. Revenue depends on distribution (how many stores stock the product), rate of sale (how fast it sells in each store) and price.

A worked example: distribution versus rate of sale

A snack is in 5,000 stores, each selling 20 packs a week at £1.50 to the retailer: £7.8M a year (5,000 × 20 × £1.50 × 52). Getting into 1,000 more stores adds about £1.6M. Raising sales per store from 20 to 24 packs adds about the same. Which is cheaper to achieve decides the strategy.

The tensions

  • Promotions lift volume but can train shoppers to buy only on deal.
  • Private label: retailers' own brands compete on the same shelf.
  • Retailer power: a few large supermarkets often control a large share of sales.

Typical consumer goods case questions

  • How should we launch a high-protein snack?
  • Why has our market share fallen?
  • Should we cut back on promotions?
outro: Next in this topic: How do airlines make money, and what matters in an airline case?
